column12: Judgement on the comparator, house convention. Tecentriq is the closest marketed comparator in the same disease and setting. It is the TIGOS control arm, and atezolizumab-based regimens were 89.5% of 2,788 US first-line ES-SCLC chemoimmunotherapy patients in Komodo claims, 2018-2023 (Le et al., Clin Lung Cancer 2026, doi:10.1016/j.cllc.2026.02.004, PMID 41904053). Imfinzi, the other first-line ES-SCLC PD-L1, reads $56,999 (Part B 2024). The case for higher: BMS-986489 is two antibodies in one vial, and Bristol's own nivolumab FDC, Opdualag (nivolumab plus relatlimab), reads $142,849 per Part B beneficiary in 2024, 1.99x Opdivo's $71,752. Pricing BMS-986489 like Opdualag would roughly double this value. The case for lower: first-line ES-SCLC patients stay on therapy for about five months (IMpower133 median PFS 5.2 months), so an SCLC beneficiary's spend is well under a year of therapy. Tecentriq's per-beneficiary figure mixes in longer adjuvant NSCLC and HCC courses. Under the house convention this figure is a per-beneficiary spend, not an annual list price

column12: Judgement on the review timeline. TIGOS is event-driven on OS: a readout around mid-2028, a BLA late in 2028 and approval around late 2029 on a standard review make 2030 the first full year. This follows the book's rule of two calendar years after primary completion (ABBV-706: September 2030 to 2032; vepugratinib: October 2029 to 2031). The case against: an OS trial can run past its estimated date, and any slip in events, filing or review makes it 2031

Ono is entitled to receive royalties of 4% in North America and 15% in all territories excluding the three countries listed above, subject to customary adjustments. Ono also receives royalties on the nivolumab component of Opdualag consistent with the terms previously stated for Opdivo.' BMS-986489 and atigotatug are not named. Bristol's J.P. Morgan deck of 12 January 2026 (8-K 0001140361-26-000929, exhibit) lists its development partnerships as 'Anti-CCR8 + nivolumab, nivolumab + relatlimab HD, OPDIVO, YERVOY: Ono; ...' and carries 'atigotatug + nivolumab, 1L Extensive-Stage Small Cell Lung Cancer' among its Phase III programmes with no partner named. Bristol is lead sponsor of NCT06646276 and NCT06799286 (book trials table)
column12: JUDGEMENT, and a ceiling. No filing names a partner, a royalty or a royalty base for BMS-986489, so the share is 1.0 under the brief's rule (from a filing, else 1.0) and the book's practice for an undisclosed royalty (ABBV-706, GSK5784283: not charged, and said so). The case against: the FDC contains nivolumab, and Bristol pays Ono 4% in North America and 15% in other territories outside Japan, South Korea and Taiwan on Opdivo, Opdivo Qvantig and the nivolumab component of Opdualag. A royalty on the nivolumab component of this FDC is therefore likely, but how that component is valued is not disclosed even for Opdualag, and neither is the royalty term. Bounds on BMY's cost rows (margin 1 - 0.2892 cogs - 0.1508 SG&A - 0.2065 R&D - 0 other = 0.3535, lookup.py seed Mavacamten) and the 0.7021 ex-US weight: the blended rate is (4% x 1.0 + 15% x 0.7021) / 1.7021 = 8.537% of revenue, so the share is 0.7585 if the royalty fell on all of the FDC's sales. The first draft's 0.8787 set the component at 0.5023 of sales, Opdivo's over Opdualag's 2024 Part B spend per beneficiary ($71,752 / $142,849). That is a spend ratio across different indications and durations, not a disclosed royalty base, so it is not used. In Japan, South Korea and Taiwan the Ono alliance shares profits equally on combinations of both parties' compounds; those markets sit outside the exus_multiple and are not modelled. The Merck patent agreement is income, not a cost: Merck pays BMS and Ono 2.5% of Keytruda sales through 2026, shared 75/25 (10-Q 0000014272-26-000020)

column11: Three filters. (1) SCLC was 11.8% of new US lung cancers in 2019, and (2) 70.9% of SCLC was extensive-stage at diagnosis over 2000-2019 (Wells et al., JTO Clin Res Rep 2025;6(4):100799, doi:10.1016/j.jtocrr.2025.100799, PMID 40104389, SEER 17). These are the book's own two filters from the ABBV-706 seed, reused. (3) 43.4% of newly diagnosed ES-SCLC patients received antineoplastic therapy: 6,838 of 15,763 in SEER-Medicare, 2001-2013 (Shah et al., JCO Oncol Pract 2020;16(7):e610-e621, doi:10.1200/JOP.19.00559, PMID 32074011). 0.118 x 0.709 x 0.4338 = 0.036293, about 8,226 first-line patients a year on the book's 226,650
column12: Judgement on filter (3). The label is first-line ES-SCLC with carboplatin and etoposide. TIGOS selects on no biomarker (fucosyl-GM1 is expressed on up to 90% of SCLC cells) and enrols ECOG 0-1, which is not expected to reach a label, so only line and stage filter. The case for higher: the 43.4% is Medicare patients aged 65 and over from 2001-2013, and it was falling to 36.6% by 2013. Younger patients are treated more often. In Flatiron's oncology-clinic population, 82% of 9,952 SCLC patients received at least one line (Shaw et al., Oncologist 2024, PMID 39349396), but patients who never see an oncologist are missing from that base. The case for keeping it: a population-based Canadian cohort found 46.5% of 1,941 ES-SCLC patients got chemotherapy (Real-World Treatment Patterns, Clinical Outcomes, and Health Care Resource Utilization in ES-SCLC in Canada, PMC8395392, located by web search and not opened), close to the SEER-Medicare figure. Book inconsistency to flag: the ABBV-706 seed applies its 13.4% third-line share to all ES-SCLC, not to treated ES-SCLC. That gives 2,540 third-line patients, 31% of the 8,226 here where its own source implies 13.4%

column11: Incumbent capture: EP plus anti-PD-L1 (atezolizumab or durvalumab) went from 7% of US first-line ES-SCLC regimens in 2018 to 68% in 2019 and about 80% by 2021 (Shaw et al., Oncologist 2024;29(12):1079-1089, doi:10.1093/oncolo/oyae234, PMID 39349396, Flatiron, 4,593 patients). Atezolizumab-based regimens were 89.5% of 2,788 first-line chemoimmunotherapy patients and durvalumab-based 10.5% (Le et al., Clin Lung Cancer 2026;27(4):41-46.e3, PMID 41904053, Komodo claims 2018-2023). Tecentriq therefore holds about 0.80 x 0.895 = 0.716 of first-line regimens
column12: JUDGEMENT: the multiple is 0.5x Tecentriq's measured capture, so 0.5 x 0.716 = 0.358, about 2,945 US patients a year at peak. The measure matches the engine's basis: with carryover 0, the peak is the share of each year's first-line patients started on the drug. The case for higher: TIGOS tests the FDC head to head against the atezolizumab regimen on OS, and chemo-PD-L1 displaced EP from 7% to 68% in a single year after IMpower133. The randomised Phase 2 reported median OS of 15.6 against 11.4 months, HR 0.71 (per search results on the TIGOS design paper; not in its PubMed abstract, so unverified). The case for lower: that Phase 2 HR's CI crossed 1 (0.44-1.16). Durvalumab, a second entrant with no head-to-head edge, took only 10.5% of chemoimmunotherapy patients. By 2030 first line will be contested by Bristol's own pumitamig (BNT327 Phase 2/3 NCT06712316, a 50/50 profit share with BioNTech, so the two partly cannibalise one another), Pfizer's PF-08634404 (NCT07226999), and tarlatamab and lurbinectedin moving into first-line maintenance
